```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.align = "center")
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(scales)
library(viridis)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
crs_m <- 26915
```

## Research question

Where in New Orleans can someone with dietary restrictions find the best halal,
vegetarian, and vegan restaurants, and which geographic area is most useful for
finding them?

## Data

```{r load-data}
business <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/business_new_orleans.rds")
reviews  <- readRDS("data/new_orleans/reviews_new_orleans.rds")
cat("Restaurants:", nrow(business), "| Reviews:", nrow(reviews), "\n")
```

The business file contains 2,259 New Orleans restaurants and the review file
contains 476,421 reviews for those restaurants. The raw Yelp JSON files were
processed in chunks during Steps 1–2 and are not required for this report.

## Step 3: Selecting related categories

I selected `halal`, `vegetarian`, and `vegan` because all three describe dietary
options that can help a diner with dietary restrictions choose a restaurant.
They are related, but they are not interchangeable: halal is a religious dietary
standard, while vegetarian and vegan describe food restrictions. A restaurant
qualifies if it matches **at least one** selected Yelp category.

```{r category-counts}
restaurant_categories <- business |>
  select(business_id, business_name, categories) |>
  separate_rows(categories, sep = ",") |>
  mutate(category = str_squish(str_to_lower(categories))) |>
  filter(category != "") |>
  distinct(business_id, business_name, category)

category_counts <- restaurant_categories |> count(category, sort = TRUE)
category_counts |> filter(category %in% c("halal", "vegetarian", "vegan"))
```

The selected categories occur on 11 halal, 70 vegetarian, and 68 vegan
business records. Because a business may have more than one label, these counts
should not be added together to estimate the number of restaurants.

```{r co-occurrence}
selected_categories <- c("halal", "vegetarian", "vegan")

selected_ids <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories) |>
  distinct(business_id)

selected_category_rows <- restaurant_categories |>
  filter(category %in% selected_categories)

selected_restaurants <- business |>
  semi_join(selected_ids, by = "business_id") |>
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude))

pair_counts <- inner_join(
  selected_category_rows,
  selected_category_rows,
  by = c("business_id", "business_name"),
  suffix = c("_a", "_b"),
  relationship = "many-to-many"
) |>
  filter(category_a < category_b) |>
  count(category_a, category_b, sort = TRUE)

pair_counts
cat("Qualifying restaurants:", nrow(selected_restaurants), "\n")
```

There are **125 qualifying restaurants**. The strongest overlap is between vegan
and vegetarian (21 businesses). Three businesses are both halal and vegetarian,
and one is both halal and vegan. Thus, the inclusion rule broadens the analysis
to restaurants offering any of the three options while still allowing overlap
to be reported transparently.

## Step 4: Joining businesses to reviews

```{r reviews}
selected_reviews <- reviews |>
  semi_join(selected_restaurants, by = "business_id") |>
  mutate(review_date = as.Date(date), review_year = lubridate::year(review_date))

business_review_summary <- selected_reviews |>
  group_by(business_id) |>
  summarise(
    reviews_in_file = n(),
    avg_review_stars = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

selected_restaurants <- selected_restaurants |>
  left_join(business_review_summary, by = "business_id")

selected_reviews |>
  summarise(
    reviews = n(),
    restaurants = n_distinct(business_id),
    reviewers = n_distinct(user_id)
  )
```

Filtering before the join leaves **29,334 reviews** from **22,665 reviewers**
for the 125 selected restaurants. The restaurant-level review average is an
ordinary mean across all available reviews; it is not a reviewer-normalized
score, because reviewer normalization is part of Step 7.

## Step 5: Official city boundary

```{r places-join}
make_points <- function(df) {
  st_as_sf(df, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326,
           remove = FALSE) |>
    st_transform(crs_m)
}

louisiana_places <- tigris::places(state = "LA", cb = TRUE, year = 2024) |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_transform(crs_m)

all_points <- make_points(filter(business, !is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)))

restaurants_with_place <- all_points |>
  st_join(louisiana_places |> select(place_geoid = GEOID,
                                     place_name = NAME),
          join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
  distinct(business_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

city_vs_place <- restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(city, place_name, sort = TRUE)
city_vs_place

mismatches <- restaurants_with_place |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(is.na(place_name) | place_name != "New Orleans") |>
  select(business_name, address, postal_code, place_name, latitude, longitude)

cat("Restaurants labeled New Orleans but outside the official polygon:",
    nrow(mismatches), "\n")
head(mismatches, 10)
```

The spatial join identifies **2,202** businesses whose Yelp city label and
official place are both New Orleans. It identifies **57 mismatches**. The
mismatches are concentrated in nearby places such as Elmwood, Jefferson, and
Harahan, with some businesses in Gretna, Terrytown, and other neighboring
communities. This pattern suggests that Yelp's `city` field often reflects a
postal or marketing address rather than the municipal polygon containing the
coordinates. I retain the Yelp-defined New Orleans restaurant set for the main
analysis, but report this boundary limitation rather than silently deleting the
mismatches.

```{r places-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
nola_boundary <- louisiana_places |> filter(NAME == "New Orleans")
nola_points <- filter(restaurants_with_place, place_name == "New Orleans")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nola_boundary, fill = "grey95", color = "grey35") +
  geom_sf(data = nola_points, aes(color = stars), alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "C", limits = c(1, 5)) +
  labs(title = "Yelp restaurants located within New Orleans",
       color = "Business\nstars") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Step 6: Choose and defend a geographic area

### Comparing geographic systems

I compare ZIP Code Tabulation Areas, Census tracts, and Census block groups.
The Census layers are downloaded through `tigris`; the points are transformed
to UTM zone 15N before joining so that all spatial layers use the same projected
coordinate system.

```{r boundaries}
zcta_raw <- tigris::zctas(cb = TRUE, starts_with = "70", year = 2020)
zip_col <- intersect(c("ZCTA5CE20", "GEOID20", "ZCTA5CE10", "GEOID10", "GEOID"),
                     names(zcta_raw))[1]
zcta <- zcta_raw |>
  st_make_valid() |> st_transform(crs_m) |>
  transmute(area_id = as.character(.data[[zip_col]]),
            area_name = paste("ZIP", area_id))

tract <- tigris::tracts(state = "LA", county = "Orleans", cb = TRUE, year = 2022) |>
  st_make_valid() |> st_transform(crs_m) |>
  transmute(area_id = GEOID, area_name = paste("Tract", NAME))

block_group <- tigris::block_groups(state = "LA", county = "Orleans", cb = TRUE,
                                    year = 2022) |>
  st_make_valid() |> st_transform(crs_m) |>
  transmute(area_id = GEOID, area_name = paste("Block group", GEOID))

systems <- list("ZIP/ZCTA" = zcta, "Census tract" = tract,
                "Census block group" = block_group)
```

```{r assign}
sel_points <- make_points(selected_restaurants)

assign_to_areas <- function(points_sf, boundary_sf) {
  points_sf |>
    st_join(boundary_sf, join = st_within, left = TRUE) |>
    st_drop_geometry() |>
    distinct(business_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
}

summarise_areas <- function(assigned) {
  assigned |>
    filter(!is.na(area_id)) |>
    group_by(area_id, area_name) |>
    summarise(
      n_restaurants = n(),
      total_reviews = sum(reviews_in_file, na.rm = TRUE),
      avg_business_stars = mean(stars, na.rm = TRUE),
      avg_review_stars = weighted.mean(avg_review_stars, reviews_in_file,
                                      na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

assigned_list <- map(systems, ~ assign_to_areas(sel_points, .x))
area_list <- map(assigned_list, summarise_areas)

comparison <- imap_dfr(assigned_list, function(a, nm) {
  s <- area_list[[nm]]
  tibble(
    `Geographic system` = nm,
    `Areas containing a selected restaurant` = nrow(s),
    `Restaurants assigned` = sum(!is.na(a$area_id)),
    `Unmatched restaurants` = sum(is.na(a$area_id)),
    `Smallest area count` = min(s$n_restaurants),
    `Median area count` = median(s$n_restaurants),
    `Largest area count` = max(s$n_restaurants),
    `Areas with 5+ restaurants` = sum(s$n_restaurants >= 5)
  )
})

knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 2,
             caption = "Comparison of geographic systems")
write_csv(comparison, "figures/geography_comparison.csv")
```

The resulting comparison is:

| Geographic system | Areas | Assigned | Unmatched | Smallest | Median | Largest | Areas with 5+ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ZIP/ZCTA | 12 | 125 | 0 | 1 | 11 | 26 | 8 |
| Census tract | 47 | 124 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 24 | 4 |
| Census block group | 64 | 124 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 10 | 4 |

ZIP/ZCTAs provide the clearest comparison for this question. They are familiar
to a general audience, have no unmatched selected restaurants, and concentrate
the restaurants into 12 areas, including eight with at least five restaurants.
The tract and block-group systems provide more geographic detail, but most
areas contain only one or two selected restaurants. Their apparent top ratings
would therefore be more sensitive to individual businesses and small samples.

```{r zip-results}
area_list[["ZIP/ZCTA"]] |>
  filter(n_restaurants >= 5) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_review_stars)) |>
  select(area_name, n_restaurants, total_reviews,
         avg_business_stars, avg_review_stars) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2,
    caption = "ZIP/ZCTA areas with at least five selected restaurants")
```

Among ZIP areas with at least five restaurants, ZIP 70112 has the highest raw
average review score (about 4.41), followed closely by ZIP 70113 (about 4.40)
and ZIP 70118 (about 4.33). ZIP 70130 has the largest number of qualifying
restaurants (26), while ZIP 70116, 70119, 70115, 70112, and 70118 also have
substantial numbers of restaurants.
This distinction matters: the area with the highest average is not necessarily
the area with the greatest choice.

```{r area-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
area_map <- zcta |>
  inner_join(area_list[["ZIP/ZCTA"]], by = c("area_id", "area_name"))

ggplot(area_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = n_restaurants), color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", na.value = "grey85") +
  labs(title = "Halal, vegetarian, and vegan restaurants by ZIP/ZCTA",
       fill = "Restaurants") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Choosing ZIP/ZCTA

I chose **ZIP/ZCTA** as the primary geographic system. ZIP areas fit the
practical question of where a visitor can look for restaurants, are easier to
interpret than Census identifiers, support a readable map, contain all 125
selected restaurants, and generally provide more stable comparisons than the
smaller tract and block-group areas. ZIP/ZCTAs do not represent neighborhoods,
and their boundaries are designed for Census tabulation rather than exact
postal delivery routes. They can also combine places that feel different on the
ground. Census tracts and block groups reveal finer spatial variation but hide
the instability caused by very small restaurant counts.

### Limitations

The main limitations are that the Yelp categories are user/platform labels and
do not independently verify that a restaurant is halal, vegetarian, or vegan.
The analysis is also observational: Yelp review volume and ratings may reflect
who chooses to review, not only restaurant quality. Several areas have only one
or a few restaurants, and the Yelp city label disagrees with the official city
polygon for 57 businesses in the full restaurant dataset. Finally, the scores
shown here are ordinary review averages and are not adjusted for reviewer
scoring habits; reviewer normalization is reserved for Step 7.
